title: Arithmetic Subarrays
statement:
Call a sequence **arithmetic** when it has two or more elements and the gap from each element to the one after it never changes; that is, `s[i + 1] - s[i] == s[1] - s[0]` holds for every valid `i`.

You get an integer array `nums` of length `n` and two integer arrays `l` and `r` of the same length `m`. Together they describe `m` queries: query `i` asks about the piece of `nums` from index `l[i]` through index `r[i]`, both ends included (all indexes are 0-based). For each query, decide whether the elements `nums[l[i]], nums[l[i] + 1], ..., nums[r[i]]` can be put in some order that makes an arithmetic sequence.

Return a list of booleans `answer` of length `m`, where `answer[i]` is `true` if query `i`'s elements can be reordered that way and `false` if they cannot.
signature: List<Boolean> checkArithmeticSubarrays(int[] nums, int[] l, int[] r)
notes:
## Intuition

A set of numbers can be arranged into an arithmetic sequence exactly when its sorted order already is one: the smallest value must come first (or last), and every gap has to be the same constant. So each query only needs its piece of `nums` sorted and its neighbouring gaps compared. With at most 500 queries over at most 500 values, sorting each piece is fast enough.

## Approach

1. For every query `q`, copy `nums[l[q]..r[q]]` and sort the copy into `sorted`.
2. Take the first gap, `sorted[1] - sorted[0]`, as the required `step`.
3. Walk the rest of `sorted`; if any gap `sorted[i] - sorted[i - 1]` differs from `step`, mark the query `false` and stop early.
4. Push the result into `answer` and return it after the last query.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [4, 6, 5, 9, 3, 7]`, `l = [0, 0, 2]`, `r = [2, 3, 5]`.

- Query 0: `[4, 6, 5]` sorts to `[4, 5, 6]`; `step = 1` and the next gap is 1, so `true`.
- Query 1: `[4, 6, 5, 9]` sorts to `[4, 5, 6, 9]`; `step = 1`, but the gap from 6 to 9 is 3, so `false`.
- Query 2: `[5, 9, 3, 7]` sorts to `[3, 5, 7, 9]`; every gap is 2, so `true`.

The answer is `[true, false, true]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n log n): each of the `m` queries sorts at most `n` values.
- Space: O(n) for the sorted copy (plus the `m` results).

## Pitfalls

- Sort a copy; sorting `nums` itself changes the pieces later queries look at.
- JavaScript's default `sort()` compares as strings; pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
- `r[q]` is inclusive, so the slice ends at `r[q] + 1`.
- Checking only `(max - min) % (k - 1) == 0` is not enough: `[1, 3, 3, 5]` passes that test but is not arithmetic.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `q` | index of the current query |
| `sorted` | the query's piece of `nums`, sorted ascending |
| `step` | the gap every neighbouring pair must have |
| `arithmetic` | whether all gaps seen so far equal `step` |
| `answer` | the list of results, one per query |

narration.2: Collect one true/false result per query.
narration.3: Handle the queries one at a time.
narration.4: Copy this query's piece of nums (r is inclusive) and sort the copy numerically.
narration.5: In sorted order the first gap fixes the step every other gap must match.
narration.6: Assume the piece is arithmetic until a gap disagrees.
narration.8: A gap that differs from step means no order can work.
